title: Zero Tail
statement: A factory stamps the serial numbers in numbers onto one big crate by multiplying them all together and writing the product in base base (digits 0 to base - 1, so base 10 is ordinary decimal). Return how many zero digits the written product ends with. The product can have tens of thousands of digits, so it must be reasoned about without building it with ordinary numbers.

examples.explanation: The product is 252000, which ends in three zeros in decimal. The numbers factor as 40 = 2^3 * 5, 75 = 3 * 5^2, 12 = 2^2 * 3 and 7, so the product holds five 2s and three 5s. A decimal zero uses one 2 and one 5, and the 5s run out after three.

The product is 1944. Since 12 = 2^2 * 3, each trailing zero in base 12 needs two 2s and one 3. The product has three 2s and five 3s, so only one zero can be formed: 1944 is written as 1 1 6 0 in base 12.

hints.content: A number ends in k zeros in some base exactly when base^k divides it. What does that say about the prime factors the product needs to contain?
Multiplying everything with BigInt and dividing by the base until it stops dividing is correct, but the product has up to about 45,000 decimal digits and may be divided over a hundred thousand times.
Split the base into prime powers by trial division up to its square root, about 31,623 at most: base = p1^e1 * p2^e2 * ...
For one prime p, count how many times p divides each number and add those counts. The product contains exactly that many copies of p.

That prime allows floor(count / e) zeros, where e is its exponent in the base. The answer is the smallest allowance over all primes of the base. Time is about O(sqrt(base) + n * log(max) * distinct primes).

testCases.explanation: Decimal case limited by the factors of 5.
A composite base with a squared prime, limited by the factors of 2.
The product is 1, which has no trailing zeros.
A large prime base that divides the single number exactly once.
A power of two base (2^29): three numbers of 2^29 give three zeros.
A base that is the product of the first nine primes; several of those primes are missing from most numbers.
Random large numbers against a base with six distinct primes and squared and fourth powers.
The largest input with 145,000 factors of 2: a BigInt product has 145,000 bits and must be divided by 2 that many times.
The largest input with numbers built from powers of 2 and 3 against base 6.
The largest input with powers of two against base 2^29, so the answer depends on integer division of the counts.

solutions.title: Build the product and divide by the base
solutions.intuition: Compute the whole product with BigInt and strip the base off the end until it no longer divides.
solutions.approach: Multiply all numbers as BigInt, then while product % base is zero, divide and count.
solutions.pseudocode:
product = 1n
for v in numbers: product *= v
zeros = 0
while product % base == 0: product //= base; zeros += 1
solutions.timeComplexity: Each division is O(size of the product); with up to 145,000 divisions of a 145,000-bit number this is hundreds of millions of word operations
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log max) bits for the product
commonMistakes: Using ordinary numbers, which lose precision after 2^53.
Checking only whether the last decimal digit is zero when the base is not 10.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the literal reading of the question, and with BigInt it is exact. The product gets enormous and every division copies it, so the work grows with the answer times the product size. The prime-count solution never builds the product.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.content: In the first example the product 40 * 75 * 12 * 7 is 252000.

steps.title: Divide
steps.content: 252000 divides by 10 three times (25200, 2520, 252) and then stops, so the answer is 3.

solutions.title: Count the base's prime factors in the product
solutions.intuition: A trailing zero in base b consumes one copy of b, i.e. e copies of each prime p with p^e exactly dividing b. The scarcest prime sets the limit.
solutions.approach: Factor the base by trial division. For each prime p with exponent e in the base, sum the exponent of p in every number, then take floor(sum / e). Return the minimum over the primes of the base.
solutions.pseudocode:
remaining = base; answer = infinity
for p = 2, 3, ... while remaining > 1 (jump to remaining when p*p > remaining):
  if p divides remaining: e = exponent of p; remaining /= p^e
    have = sum over numbers of exponent of p in the number
    answer = min(answer, floor(have / e))
return answer
solutions.timeComplexity: O(sqrt(base) + n * (log max + distinct primes of base))
commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide the prime's count by its exponent in the base.
Taking the maximum instead of the minimum across the primes.
Stopping trial division at sqrt(base) and missing a large prime left over in remaining.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The product is divisible by base^k exactly when, for every prime power p^e in the base, the product has at least k * e copies of p. So the answer is the minimum over primes of floor(copies / e). Factoring the base costs at most about 31,623 trial divisions, and counting copies over 5,000 numbers is cheap, so nothing larger than a 32-bit integer is ever created.

steps.title: Count and compare
steps.content: The numbers 40, 75, 12 and 7 contain five 2s and three 5s, giving allowances of 5 and 3, so the answer is 3.
